back: Two firms agree to join together to form one business, normally by an exchange of shares.
One firm buys enough shares of another to gain control of it. It is friendly if the target's board agrees and hostile if the board resists.
Joining a firm at the same stage of production in the same industry, for example a bakery buying a bakery.
Joining a firm at a different stage of the supply chain: backward towards suppliers, forward towards customers.
Joining firms in unrelated industries, mainly to spread risk.

front: Why mergers and takeovers may fail
back: Clash of cultures, diseconomies of scale, overpaying, integration problems and loss of key staff.
A joint venture is a new project or company owned by two or more firms; a strategic alliance is a cooperation agreement without a merger. Both share cost and risk but reduce control.
Market share (%) = firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100. After a merger, add the two firms' sales.
Shareholders may gain or overpay; workers may face redundancy; customers may lose choice; suppliers gain a bigger customer or lose one; competitors face a stronger rival.
